title: Upasiva's question
hook: one of the sixteen asks what to rely on to cross; the Buddha answers, nothingness, mindfully

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old teacher's sixteen students on the road north, and your line, crossing the flood. Did you carry your question around with you? Today, one of the sixteen asks his. Day six hundred ten.

Upasiva is the sixth of the sixteen to speak. His question is short, and it's the most honest thing anyone says in the whole chapter. Alone, he says, with nothing to hold on to, I can't cross the great flood. Tell me something to lean on. Anyone who has stood at the edge of something too big, a diagnosis, a debt, a loss, knows that sentence. Not what is the meaning of life. Just: what do I hold? Today: Upasiva's question.
screen: `THE SIXTH OF THE SIXTEEN.` → `ALONE, I CAN'T CROSS.` → `TELL ME SOMETHING TO LEAN ON.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer is surprising. Mindful, he says, looking to nothingness, leaning on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense-desires, step back from talk, and watch, day and night, for the end of craving. Upasiva had meditated deeply; the commentary says he already knew the meditation called the base of nothingness. So the Buddha meets him there, in the place he already knows, and adds the one thing that turns it from a resting place into a crossing: mindfulness. Upasiva asks more. If someone stays there, does he go cold, or is he freed? The Buddha gives an image. As a flame blown out by the wind goes to rest and can't be counted any more, so the sage, freed, goes to rest and can't be counted. Does he not exist then, Upasiva asks, or is he forever well? There's no measuring the one who has gone to rest, the Buddha says. When everything is uprooted, every way of speaking about him is uprooted too. That last answer is famous because it refuses both easy options. And with it, we close the Sutta Nipata: from the snake shedding its skin, through the herdsman in the rain, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the blessings, the poet, the dart, the eights, all the way to this crossing. Tomorrow, a new book, of joy.
screen: `MINDFUL, LOOKING TO NOTHINGNESS.` · `MEETING HIM WHERE HE IS.` · `A FLAME BLOWN OUT BY THE WIND.` · `NO MEASURING THE ONE AT REST.` · then, large: `MINDFUL, CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rely on mindfulness today. Sit and settle. Notice what you usually lean on when things get hard: your phone, a plan, someone's reassurance. You don't have to give any of them up. Just, for these two minutes, lean on nothing but knowing what's happening. Breath in, known. Breath out, known. A sound, known. When the mind reaches for a handhold, notice the reaching, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Upasiva's question. One of the sixteen asks what to lean on to cross the flood, and is told: mindful, looking to nothingness, cross. Today's word.
Your line: mindful, cross. Today, when something feels too big, take one step with full attention, and let that step be enough. Day six hundred ten.

howItsDone: Teachers often cite Upasiva's question when explaining nibbana as the flame gone out, and the image of the flame that can no longer be reckoned is common in Theravada teaching on what can and cannot be said of the awakened.

fork.setup: Upasiva asks: is the freed one gone, or forever well? what does the Buddha say?
options: there's no measuring him; the ways of speaking are uprooted.
fork.reveal: he refuses both options. like a flame gone out, the freed one can't be counted in the old terms.

original.note: Pali ogha: a flood. crossing the ogha is the image that runs through the Parayana.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana means being snuffed out.
what it means: in Sn 5.7 the flame gone out can't be measured; neither 'he is not' nor 'he is forever' fits.
what a scholar hears: Sn 5.7 uses the fire simile (accī yathā vātavegena khitto) for the arahant who can't be reckoned (na upeti sankham).

notes: Sn 5.7 paraphrased. Confirm the order of Upasiva's three questions and the flame simile.
That Upasiva already knew the base of nothingness comes from the commentary (Niddesa / Paramatthajotika); confirm.
Readings differ on 'looking to nothingness' (akincanna): as the formless attainment used as a support, or more broadly as 'nothing' to hold. The script follows the commentary's reading.
This day closes the Sutta Nipata section (days 576–610) and points to the Udana.
